caseStudy.subtitle: Engineering a streaming platform across web and connected TV.

metadata.label: Domains
metadata.value: Streaming, Commerce, DRM, Blockchain, Connected TV

sections.title: The product
sections.body:
DCP+ is Decentralized Pictures’ streaming platform for films and episodic content. It brings catalogue discovery, rentals, purchases, subscriptions, and advertising-supported viewing into a single experience, with protected playback across web and connected TV.

The familiar act of choosing a title and pressing play crosses several systems: viewer identity, card payments, wallet signing, blockchain settlement, content entitlements, and DRM-protected media. My work connected those boundaries into a usable client application. A successful journey meant that viewers could find content, understand their access, complete a transaction, and watch with progress retained for their next session.

sections.title: My engagement
sections.body:
I joined DCP+ through Lazer Technologies in June 2025, embedded within the client’s engineering team. Working alongside product and engineering stakeholders, I helped refine requirements, translate product goals into application behavior, and resolve the integration questions that stood between implementation and a working viewer experience.

From August 2025, I was the primary engineer responsible for the client applications. My scope covered application architecture, feature and integration ownership, technical investigations, connected TV, operational tooling, and release preparation. That responsibility required moving between product details and system behavior: understanding what a viewer needed to accomplish, deciding where the application should own that behavior, and collaborating across service boundaries to make it work.

I carried that approach through catalogue and account experiences, commerce, playback, and episodic viewing. The goal was a coherent product whose parts could evolve together, with maintainable contracts between the interface and the services behind it.

sections.title: Application architecture
sections.body:
I restructured the application around explicit route boundaries to make session responsibilities predictable. Global providers had allowed unrelated dependencies to interact, producing inconsistent request initialization and flashes of content before redirects. Each route needed a clear answer to what session, permissions, and data had to be ready before its experience could proceed.

The resulting structure separated root infrastructure, authentication routes, the main streaming session, and page-local data and permissions. This gave initialization a clearer order and reduced coupling between experiences. Application lifecycle work, including bounded recovery and cleanup, also addressed repeated SDK initialization and made recovery behavior easier to reason about.

Generated OpenAPI types and view models stabilized the interface as API contracts evolved. Generated types exposed contract changes during development, while mapping code kept endpoint-specific shapes out of presentation components. Those boundaries supported discovery, profiles, personal libraries, and series and episode experiences without tying every component directly to a service response.

The Next.js backend-for-frontend provided another deliberate boundary, moving session tokens into HttpOnly cookies with CSRF protection. Together, these decisions made access, data readiness, and lifecycle management explicit responsibilities within the application.

sections.title: Commerce and authentication
sections.body:
Wallet signing helped establish a viewer session, but continuous wallet connectivity was unnecessary for browsing and playback. When unexpected sign-outs appeared, targeted telemetry showed restoration failures while the wallet SDK was still connecting. I used that evidence to reconsider the dependency instead of simply adding more reconnection attempts.

I made the viewer session the authority for application authentication and treated the wallet as an on-demand signing capability. This separated access to the streaming experience from the availability of a wallet for a particular purchase, subscription, or renewal operation. In-place signing recovery let the viewer address a wallet problem within the transaction workflow.

Commerce required similarly clear boundaries. I implemented Stripe purchasing, wallet-signed transactions, subscriptions, and reusable payment methods, connecting the interface to the steps needed for access. Payment completion, blockchain settlement, and a playable entitlement could arrive separately; showing them as one event produced misleading calls to action and indefinite pending states.

I consolidated five sources of client settlement state into a unified transaction state machine. It gave the application one consistent model of progress, including a longer-than-usual state, while preserving the distinction between paying for content and being able to play it. That made the client workflow clearer and gave technical investigations a more precise starting point.

sections.title: Playback and connected TV
sections.body:
I integrated DRM-protected playback with FairPlay and Widevine across HLS and DASH delivery, then built the surrounding experience: custom controls, audio and subtitle selection, progress tracking, resume, and playback recovery. The work extended beyond displaying video to maintaining a consistent viewing session across browsers and devices.

Safari exposed a difficult authorization boundary. Protected content played in Chrome, but Safari’s native HLS path did not carry the expected authorization headers. Playlist tokens did not propagate as needed, cross-site cookies were dropped, and alternative playback paths did not resolve FairPlay decryption. Working with the client’s engineering team, I helped establish a functioning path using signed CDN cookies, a CDN alias on the application’s site, and appropriate CORS configuration.

Later compatibility work introduced an iOS 17.1 and newer path using Managed Media Source for authorization injection with FairPlay support. Playback recovery also became a product interaction: Watch Here let a viewer reclaim playback after another session took over.

A shared TypeScript core carried API clients, view models, session logic, streaming behavior, and error handling across web and TV. I built the Samsung Tizen experience around those foundations, with device sign-in and remote navigation adapted to television use. A signed build passed Samsung Seller Office pre-testing in June 2026, establishing a tested distribution path toward store submission.

sections.title: Delivery and reflection
sections.body:
The engagement produced a live streaming web product and an end-to-end purchase-to-playback journey. A real purchase settled on-chain and became playable in March 2026. Safari DRM playback followed in April, the web service and Cannes beta in May, and a production web release in July. In October, I prepared the v0.3.0 release package, bringing together later work on episodic content, subscriptions, advertising, settlement, and recovery.

Additional contributions made the product easier to operate. I implemented VAST advertising behavior that allowed content to continue when inventory was empty or ad requests failed. Localization automation connected a scoped Laravel import endpoint to CI publishing, using merge-safe updates and translation diagnostics to replace manual resource imports in development and staging.

This work reinforced how much reliable delivery depends on understanding the complete product journey. Clear route responsibilities, explicit transaction state, and evidence-led playback investigations made complex integrations easier to explain and maintain. Being embedded in the team let me connect those technical decisions to product requirements and carry them through implementation, validation, and release preparation.

caseStudy.subtitle: Engineering DeFi products around wallet identity, smart contracts, and financial workflows.

sections.title: Understanding the financial product
sections.body:
Concrete Finance brings financial products built around blockchain-based vaults and smart contracts into a user-facing application. A user needs to understand a position, connect an account, authorize an operation, and interpret the resulting financial information. Those steps belong to one product journey even though they cross the interface, the wallet, and the blockchain.

My engagement covered two distinct products. I took full ownership of the frontend implementation of Concrete Earn, connecting wallet identity, vault interactions, and portfolio management. On Concrete Borrow, I worked alongside other engineers on multi-network vault management, liquidation protection features, APY visibility, and reusable integrations. The products shared a need for understandable financial workflows, but my responsibilities were different in each.

sections.title: Taking ownership of Concrete Earn
sections.body:
Concrete Earn was a complete product responsibility. I owned the client implementation from wallet connection and authentication through vault discovery, deposits, withdrawals, rewards, balances, and portfolio views. The work required understanding how each interaction related to the financial operation underneath it.

I integrated directly with smart contracts to retrieve on-chain data and execute user-authorized transactions. The application therefore had to connect two kinds of interaction: reading information about an account or vault, and asking the user to authorize an operation that would change blockchain state.

A deposit or withdrawal was part of a larger experience. Users also needed to see the relevant vault information, understand their balances and positions, and return to a portfolio view that made those holdings meaningful. Owning the complete implementation let me work across those connections rather than treating each screen as an isolated delivery.

sections.title: Wallet identity and transaction authorization
sections.body:
The wallet experience used Web3Auth and WalletConnect. My responsibility included connection flows and wallet-based authentication and authorization, bringing the connected account into the application’s financial workflows.

Connection, identity, and transaction authorization are related, but they answer different questions. Connectivity establishes access to a wallet; the account identifies whose information the application is working with; signing authorizes a particular blockchain operation. A connected wallet does not by itself authorize every action the interface can present.

Keeping those distinctions clear mattered when connecting a product action to a contract call. Reading a balance and submitting a deposit should not be treated as interchangeable interactions. The latter requires explicit user signing, so authorization is part of the experience the application has to communicate.

sections.title: Connecting product actions to smart contracts
sections.body:
I built the Earn application with React, Next.js, and TypeScript, integrating its financial workflows directly with smart contracts. Contract reads supplied vault information, balances, rewards, and portfolio data. Deposits and withdrawals connected user intent in the interface to signed transactions.

Reading contract state gives the application information to present. Submitting a transaction asks the blockchain system to change that state. That distinction shaped the responsibility at the integration boundary: the interface needed to represent what was known about a position while making the operation being authorized understandable.

This work went beyond consuming a conventional API for every financial action. I had to connect the financial meaning of the interaction to the contract operation and the connected account, then carry that relationship through the user-facing workflow. The integration and the product experience were parts of the same implementation.

sections.title: Making financial information usable
sections.body:
Balances, rewards, vault positions, and portfolio views gave users different perspectives on their holdings. A vault interaction focuses attention on one operation; a portfolio view helps someone understand their position across the product. I implemented both as parts of the Earn experience.

The product challenge was to make that information readable without hiding the transaction requirements behind it. A balance provides context for a decision, while transaction feedback helps explain the action the user is taking. Clear presentation matters because the interface is where people relate a financial intention to an operation they must authorize.

That made financial information a core engineering concern. Retrieving on-chain values was only part of the work; those values also had to serve the deposit, withdrawal, rewards, and portfolio journeys that brought users to the application.

sections.title: Contributing to Concrete Borrow
sections.body:
Concrete Borrow was a separate collaboration with other engineers. My contributions covered multi-network vault management, liquidation protection features, APY visibility, and reusable SDK modules for partner integrations.

These workflows brought a different set of product considerations. Liquidation-related information matters to how users understand a borrowing position and the protection features available to them. APY visibility gives users financial information relevant to interpreting the product. My work connected these capabilities to the user experience within the wider team’s implementation.

I also developed reusable SDK modules for partner integrations. Reusable integration code gives product surfaces a common way to connect with capabilities instead of requiring each surface to assemble its own integration. This extended my contribution beyond the immediate interface while keeping the focus on the financial workflows the products needed to support.

sections.title: What financial application ownership taught me
sections.body:
This engagement reinforced that a useful financial interface starts with understanding the operation itself. Wallet connectivity, account identity, contract reads, and signed transactions all participate in the experience, but they carry different responsibilities.

Owning Earn meant keeping those responsibilities connected across a complete product. Contributing to Borrow meant applying the same care within a shared implementation. In both, the work I value most is the connection between maintainable integrations and clear financial information: users need to understand what they are looking at and what they are authorizing.

metadata.label: Integrations

sections.title: Building the application from scratch
sections.body:
In March 2023, I began work on a greenfield AI research application at Reka AI. Users could supply their own data for model fine-tuning and interact with customized models through a conversational interface. The application connected model customization with the experience of using the resulting model.

As the sole client-side engineer, I established the application and implemented its core user-facing experiences. My responsibility was to turn the capabilities exposed by the underlying services into a coherent product: access the application, provide data for customization, and carry on a conversation with a model.

That ownership sat at the client boundary. The AI models and training infrastructure belonged to the underlying services; my work made those capabilities accessible through the application and connected the workflows users needed to move between them.

sections.title: Making token-based access part of the experience
sections.body:
Users required an assigned token to access the application. I implemented the client experience around that access model, making token-based authentication the entry point to the research workflows.

Access was part of the product journey rather than a separate piece of plumbing. Before a user could work with data or interact with a customized model, the application needed to connect their access token with the services that supported those experiences. This gave the client a clear responsibility at the start of the workflow without making it the owner of the underlying model infrastructure.

sections.title: Connecting user data to model fine-tuning
sections.body:
Model fine-tuning was central to the product. I integrated Python APIs that exposed the customization capabilities, connecting the user-facing data-supply workflow to the services responsible for fine-tuning.

The client work was about making that capability usable as a sequence of related actions. Users supplied data for customization and could then interact with the resulting models. The application had to connect those experiences so that model customization led into an actual conversation, rather than leaving fine-tuning as an isolated technical operation.

The API boundary defined what the application could request and what information it could present. Working closely with those contracts was essential to representing the research capabilities accurately. I implemented the client integrations and workflows; the Python services performed the underlying fine-tuning work.

sections.title: Presenting a conversation as it unfolds
sections.body:
I built the conversational interface through which users interacted with fine-tuned models. Responses appeared progressively as output arrived, rather than waiting for an entire response before showing it.

Streaming changed the interaction from a single request followed by a finished result into an ongoing exchange. The client had to display an answer that was still arriving while maintaining the context of the conversation. Managing that ongoing conversation was part of the application’s responsibility, alongside presenting the model output itself.

For this product, the chat experience completed the customization journey. Supplying data and fine-tuning a model had a tangible destination: users could converse with the customized model and examine its responses through the same application.

sections.title: Connecting the research workflow
sections.body:
The core experiences needed to work together: token-based access, supplying data for fine-tuning, and interacting with customized models. I worked across those boundaries as one client application, connecting the services to the actions users could take.

Conversation management belonged in that larger workflow. The interface needed to support an ongoing exchange with the model, while the fine-tuning integration gave the conversation its customization context. Keeping the relationship between data, model customization, and conversation visible was more useful than presenting each backend capability as a disconnected tool.

sections.title: Engineering an AI interface in 2023
sections.body:
This work took place during an early period of widespread experimentation with generative AI products. Many interaction conventions and large-context capabilities that became more familiar later were still developing. The practical question was how to make the particular research capabilities available through this application understandable to its users.

The engineering work connected access control, model customization, and streaming responses. It required close attention to backend API contracts and an interface that could represent evolving research capabilities. As the sole client-side engineer, I carried that translation across the application rather than working on only one isolated feature.

sections.title: What I took from the engagement
sections.body:
Building this application from an early stage taught me to look for the user journey connecting specialized services. A fine-tuning capability becomes useful to a user through the actions around it: gaining access, supplying data, and interacting with the model that results.

The streaming interface made that lesson particularly concrete. The application was responsible for an experience that continued while the service was producing output. I came away with a stronger appreciation for defining the client’s responsibilities clearly and building conversational interactions around what the underlying services could actually deliver.
